title: Was Cleopatra Really Killed by an Asp? None of the 3 Ancient Writers Saw It
description:
You've surely seen it: Cleopatra dying with an asp in her arms. This episode covers only what the records hold, following her last days as Plutarch's Life of Antony tells them: the wounded Antony hauled up by rope to the tomb's high window; Octavian wanting her alive for the treasure and his triumph; an envoy climbing in through the window and seizing her dagger; her refusing food for a time; a steward exposing her treasure list; Dolabella sending word that she would be sent away within three days; offerings at the tomb; a bath and a meal; the basket of figs the guard had looked over; a sealed letter; the shut door. Plutarch gives the snake under the figs, the snake in a vessel and the hollow hairpin as "some say," and says outright that no one knows what really took place; Cassius Dio's Roman History also says no one knows for sure, noting only faint marks on her arm, a snake in a water jar or among flowers, and a poisoned pin; Suetonius's Life of Augustus says she was "supposed" to have been bitten by an asp, which is why Octavian had Psylli try to suck out the poison. The statue of the queen with a snake in the triumphal parade proves the snake version became a public image of victory, not that anyone saw a bite. A snakebite is possible, but unconfirmed.

Limits: all three writers wrote after the events, not as witnesses inside the tomb; this episode relies on Project Gutenberg's English translations, the quotes in the video are paraphrases, and the Greek and Latin originals were not checked. Sources are listed under References below.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated; the historical figures are cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant as likenesses; no asp is shown biting the queen, and no version is drawn as a definite death scene.

Information as of 2026-10-20 (rewritten under the new rules on 2026-10-25)

chapters.open-you: A guard stops a basket of figs
chapters.seal: A letter sent, the door shut
chapters.dio-look: Dio: faint marks on the arm

kp101.text: You've surely seen it: Cleopatra holds an asp and dies, just like that.

kp102.text: Behind the shut door: only her and two maids,

kp103.text: and not one lived to tell what happened inside.

kp104.text: In Alexandria, the Romans held Cleopatra under guard inside a tomb.

kp105.text: A peasant came up with a small basket of figs;

kp106.text: The guard stopped him: what's inside?

kp107.text: Stranger still: later, a triumphal parade carried a statue of the queen with a snake.

kp108.text: This file retraces her last days as three ancient writers tell them: three books, one door.

kp109.text: Did an asp really kill Cleopatra?

kp201.text: Before the guards came, that tomb was shut from inside: she had moved her treasure in, and herself too.

kp202.text: Then the wounded Antony was carried to that door.

kp203.text: Still shut. From a high window, she and her maids hauled him up on ropes.

kp204.text: Picture it: a few women, hauling a wounded grown man all the way up.

kp205.text: Plutarch writes that Antony died at her side.

kp206.text: Reading this, I think: all she had left was a tomb, a pile of treasure, and a door.

kp207.text: What did the Romans outside the door want?

kp208.text: Plutarch says Octavian, afraid to lose the treasure, wanted her alive.

kp209.text: Suetonius agrees: Octavian wanted her alive, to display in his triumph.

kp210.text: Put simply, as these two writers tell it, a living queen was worth most to him.

kp211.text: He sent a man named Proculeius to talk at the door.

kp212.text: She talked through the door but wouldn't open it. Did he have a way?

kp213.text: He did. He looked up and saw that high window: the very one Antony was pulled through.

kp214.text: Another envoy, Gallus, kept her talking at the door;

kp215.text: Proculeius and two men set up a ladder, climbed in the window, and rushed to her.

kp216.text: She reached out and found a dagger.

kp217.text: Think she made it in time?

kp301.text: She didn't. Proculeius seized the dagger, and searched her clothes for poison.

kp302.text: Remember that word, poison: it'll be back.

kp304.text: with orders: be courteous, but never let her kill herself.

kp305.text: But Plutarch notes something else: she stopped eating.

kp306.text: Plutarch says this comes from her doctor, Olympus.

kp308.text: No. He threatened her children; she started eating again.

kp309.text: A cold move, but you have to admit it worked.

kp310.text: Later Octavian came in person. She rose from her bed and pleaded with him.

kp311.text: She said she had feared Antony, defending her past choices; Octavian refuted each point.

kp312.text: She changed her tone and begged, as if she wanted to live longer.

kp314.text: She then gave him a treasure list;

kp315.text: but a steward jumped in: some things weren't on it.

kp316.text: Furious, she grabbed the steward by the hair.

kp317.text: You know that fury when a coworker calls you out on the spot? I don't condone what she did, but I get it.

kp318.text: But who were the missing items meant for?

kp319.text: She said they were small gifts, so Octavian's family would plead for her.

kp320.text: Octavian let her keep them, and promised to treat her better.

kp321.text: He concluded: at last, she wanted to live.

kp322.text: But here Plutarch adds a line: he was deceived.

kp323.text: Reading that gave me a chill.

kp324.text: So what was she really planning?

kp401.text: She had already enlisted a young man in Octavian's circle.

kp402.text: He was Dolabella, and at her request he secretly sent word.

kp403.text: To me, this is the most spy-movie part of the whole file.

kp404.text: Octavian would go home via Syria; within three days, she and her children would be sent off.

kp405.text: Three days left, in her shoes: what would you do first?

kp406.text: She asked to make offerings at Antony's tomb. This time, Octavian agreed.

kp407.text: She was taken to the tomb, her women beside her.

kp408.text: The biography has her plead there: not to be taken far away, but buried with Antony.

kp409.text: But she'd soon be taken from Egypt; who could promise her that?

kp410.text: She laid a wreath, kissed the tomb, and went back.

kp411.text: Once back, she first ordered a bath;

kp412.text: after it, she ate a lavish meal.

kp413.text: If you were the guard at the door, you'd likely relax: a bath, a meal, like she meant to go on living.

kp414.text: And just then, someone came to the door.

kp415.text: Remember the basket of figs stopped at the start? It arrived now.

kp416.text: He parted the leaves for the guard: nothing but figs.

kp417.text: The guard praised the big, fine figs, but took none.

kp418.text: The basket went in; the guard stayed out. Inside, what did she do next?

kp501.text: She wrote a letter, sealed it, and sent it to Octavian.

kp502.text: Then she sent everyone out, keeping only Iras and Charmion.

kp504.text: From here on, every word you and I read was written afterward, by others.

kp505.text: Octavian opened her letter: "Bury me with Antony."

kp506.text: One read, and he guessed the worst.

kp507.text: He rose to go but changed his mind and sent others.

kp508.text: The door guard still noticed nothing. Would they make it?

kp509.text: When the door opened, she was already dead, dressed in royal robes.

kp510.text: Iras lay dying at the bed's foot; Charmion was still fixing the queen's diadem.

kp511.text: Plutarch says Charmion gave the men one reply, then collapsed too.

kp512.text: Every time I read this, the quiet chills me.

kp513.text: As for her plea at the tomb: Octavian later let her be buried with Antony,

kp514.text: and ordered her women buried too. I think it's the one thing in this whole story she surely got.

kp515.text: The messengers saw only the result. So how did she actually die?

kp601.text: The best-known version involves the fig basket.

kp602.text: Some say the snake hid under the figs;

kp603.text: she moved the fruit, saw it, and held out her arm to be bitten.

kp604.text: That's probably the scene you grew up with.

kp605.text: But note: Plutarch writes "some say," not "the guard saw."

kp606.text: All the guard saw were figs.

kp607.text: Others say the snake was in a vessel, and she poked it with a golden spindle.

kp608.text: This version doesn't even need the basket.

kp610.text: One version says the poison was hidden in her coiled hair: in a hollow hairpin.

kp611.text: Side by side, can the marks on her body help us choose one?

kp612.text: Plutarch says no clear signs of poison showed, and no snake was found in the tomb.

kp613.text: Some say tracks like a snake's were seen in the sand by the sea;

kp614.text: others say her arm had two faint dots.

kp615.text: He records both only as "some say."

kp616.text: So which one did Plutarch himself believe?

kp617.text: He picked none, and wrote only: what really took place is known to no one.

kp618.text: Remember the door at the start? No one inside lived to tell,

kp619.text: so even the most detailed writer can only admit it. Honestly, it stunned me the first time.

kp620.text: But let me be clear: no snake found doesn't mean no snake.

kp621.text: Can Cassius Dio, who wrote a Roman History, fill the gap?

kp701.text: He can't. Dio, too, begins: no one knows for sure how she died.

kp702.text: Odder still, he and Plutarch differ even on where she was held.

kp703.text: Dio says she was moved to the palace, with her usual staff.

kp704.text: He adds that she gave away precious jewels and said she'd gladly sail, so her guards relaxed.

kp705.text: See, that's far from Plutarch's version, where she's searched and watched closely.

kp706.text: Some details match: Dio also has the sealed letter, and the clothes she changed into last.

kp707.text: Dio also describes the body: on the arm, only faint marks.

kp708.text: From that alone, could you tell a snake's fang from a pin?

kp709.text: You can't. He just lists the claims: some say the snake hid in a water jar, or in flowers;

kp710.text: others say she nicked her arm and touched a poisoned pin to the blood.

kp711.text: Even on the hairpin, the books disagree: one hides poison inside, one smears it on.

kp712.text: What did Octavian think when he arrived and saw her?

kp802.text: Suetonius, the third writer, is more specific: Octavian had Psylli try to suck out the poison;

kp803.text: because she was "supposed" to have died of an asp bite.

kp804.text: Dio describes these Psylli too, their powers almost magical; that's ancient belief, not medicine.

kp805.text: You may think: they tried sucking out venom, so it was a snake?

kp807.text: sending them only shows that some thought so then.

kp808.text: Nor does his book say Octavian saw a snake himself.

kp809.text: Octavian never got to lead her alive in his triumph. So was she missing from it?

kp810.text: No. Remember the statue of the queen with a snake from the start? Plutarch says it was in this very parade.

kp811.text: It proves one thing: the snake version had become Rome's public image of victory.

kp812.text: But carving a snake doesn't mean anyone saw a snake bite.

kp813.text: Side by side, what you see isn't three witnesses, but how one legend forked.

kp814.text: My take: what people remember is often the version that got paraded.

kp815.text: So was she killed by an asp or not?

kp816.text: So the verdict: an asp bite is possible, but the record can't support saying it surely killed her.

kp817.text: What did you picture: the basket snake, or the parade statue? Tell me below.

kp818.text: This channel sticks to what's on record. Subscribe to open the files with me.
